latin.263: CAPUT V. Examen Cap. III. In quo disquiritur, Quid sit imputari vel non imputari peccatum. Capite tertio rursus constituis statum controversiae, eoque constituto iterum digrederis, ac tibi sumis illustrandum, quid sit imputare & imputari, ac primum verbum hebraeum, deinde verbum graecum expendis, laudatis in eum finem aliquot Scripturae locis: quorsum, aut quo consilio, nescio, nisi forte, ut tui tractatus molem augeres, ac tuorum argumentorum paucitatem tegeres: utilis quidem fortasse tua haec illustratio foret ad controversiam de justificatione: quoniam Scriptura eam solita est modo imputatione fidei & justitiae, modo non imputatione peccati describere: ad hanc vero, quae inter nos agitur, quaestionem quid valeat non video: Nullus enim extat in tota Scriptura locus, in quo peccatum Adami nobis imputari dicatur.
latin.264: Itaque non quaeritur inter nos, quo sensu Scriptura usurpet in hac quaestione verbum imputandi; nunquam enim usurpat, sed quo sensu in meis thesibus (quandoquidem tu eas refutare aggressus es) negaverim peccatum Adami nobis imputari, ut mea illa negatio, qualis sit, verane an falsa cognoscatur, ac vitetur παραλογισμός. Tandem concludis, peccatum imputari, cum attribuitur, consideratur, & pro peccato habetur & punitur ut peccatum; Ex opposito peccatum non imputari, cum non consideratur ut peccatum, sed tegitur, condonatur & remittitur. Quod certe non est accommodatum ad quaestionem nostram.
latin.265: Cum enim affirmo, peccatum actuale Adami nobis non imputari, non hoc volo peccatum illud non considerari ut peccatum, sed tegi, condonari, & remitti nobis. (vides alienam esse hanc tuam non imputandi explicationem a mea mente, & ab hac quaestione,) non quaeritur inter nos, utrum peccatum Adami nobis condonetur: talis non imputatio est a misericordia; sed quaeritur inter nos, utrum de jure, ex justitia nobis imputetur, necne? Tu proculdubio statuis non imputari, hoc est, remitti fidelibus: attamen idem contendis me adversus omnibus hominibus imputari, & quidem ita imputari, ut in omnibus puniatur actu: non quaero hoc loco quomodo ista punitio consistat cum justificatione seu remissione, & non imputatione illius peccati.
latin.266: Sed, quicquid sit, Contendo peccatum illud Adami actuale nostrum peccatum non esse. Itaque nobis jure imputari non posse. Fateor imputare esse tribuere, attribuere, adscribere: sed quaedam sunt hoc loco observanda, in primis distinctio illa imputationis in antecedentem & consequentem seu immediatam & mediatam, quam, dum statum quaestionis constituerem, Cap. 2. explicavi, nec hic repeto: ejus ut memineris te rogo. Deinde illud etiam cogitationi nostrae obversari debet, agi inter nos de imputatione non qualibet, sed judiciaria, quam punitio justa sequatur.
latin.267: Est autem ejusmodi imputatio peccati, actus judicis sententia sua peccatum alicui tribuentis, hoc est, aliquem certi cujusdam peccati reum esse pronunciantis, ac propterea poena afficiendum. Tribuitur autem alicui peccatum vel tanquam peccatori, vel tanquam peccatoris personam ultro sustinenti, vadi: illi ut suum, huic ut alienum. Nobis si peccatum Adami actuale imputatur, tribuitur, non ut alienum, sed ut nostrum: suam enim quisque nostrum, cum concipitur & nascitur, personam, non Adami, cujus vas non est, gerit.
latin.268: Considera igitur mecum, quaeso, & perpende, quomodo nobis peccatum illud primum actuale, possit imputari vere an falso, juste an injuste? Fuit actio quaedam singularis, quae non potuit reum peragere, nisi aut imperantem, aut exequentem, aut consentientem. Eam autem neque imperavimus, aut suasimus Adamo, neque ipsi, qui non eramus, commisimus, neque ei, vel antequam essemus, vel in utero materno delitescentes actu consensimus. Dic igitur, amabo te, quomodo nobis vere & juste singulis attribuatur & adscribatur? Si respondeas, vitium illud haereditarium, quod ab illa actione productum in nos manavit, esse peccati illius veluti reliquias & semen, & habitualem, ut ita loquar, voluntatis nostrae consensum; Itaque jure nobis imputari, descendes in meam sententiam, qui imputationem mediatam, quae haereditariam corruptionem sequatur, & in ea fundata sit, ultro agnosco, & doceo.

pass_a.263: CAPUT V examines Cap. III on what it is for sin to be imputed or not imputed. Having again laid down the state of the controversy in your third chapter, you digress once more and set yourself to explain imputare and imputari, first treating the Hebrew term and then the Greek, with several Scripture citations brought in for that purpose. I cannot tell to what end or plan you do this—unless it is to enlarge your tract and cloak how few arguments you actually have. That kind of illustration might help the justification debate, because Scripture often paints justification either by imputing faith and righteousness or by not imputing sin; but for the dispute between us I see no use in it, since Scripture nowhere says Adam's sin is imputed to us.
pass_a.264: So the point between us is not Scripture's sense of the verb 'to impute' in this question—Scripture never uses it here—but the sense in which my theses (which you have undertaken to refute) denied that Adam's sin is imputed to us, so that one may tell whether that denial is true or false and avoid παραλογισμός. You end by saying sin is imputed when it is attributed, considered, counted as sin, and punished as sin; and that on the contrary sin is not imputed when it is not considered as sin but is covered, forgiven, and remitted. That account is certainly not suited to our question.
pass_a.265: When I say Adam's actual sin is not imputed to us, I am not saying that sin fails to be regarded as sin and is instead covered, pardoned, and remitted to us. You can see that your reading of 'not imputing' is foreign to my meaning and to this dispute. We are not asking whether Adam's sin is forgiven us—that sort of non-imputation comes from mercy. We are asking whether, of right and from justice, it is imputed to us or not. You surely hold that it is not imputed, meaning it is remitted to believers; yet against me you also urge that it is imputed to every human being, and so imputed that in every one it is punished in act. I am not here asking how that punishment can stand with justification or remission and the non-imputation of that sin.
pass_a.266: Be that as it may, my contention is that Adam's actual sin is not our sin, and therefore cannot justly be imputed to us. I admit that to impute is to assign, attribute, or charge to someone's account; yet several points must be kept in view here. Chief among them is the Cap. 2 distinction of imputation into antecedent and consequent—that is, immediate and mediate—which I set out when I fixed the state of the question and will not restate now; please keep it in mind. Further, what should stand before our thought is that we are dealing not with imputation in any loose sense, but with judicial imputation, the kind that a just punishment follows.
pass_a.267: Imputation of sin of that kind is a judge's act whereby, by his sentence, he ascribes sin to someone—declaring him guilty of a definite sin and therefore liable to penalty. Sin is ascribed to a person either as to a sinner, or as to one who of his own accord bears the sinner's person as a surety: to the first as his own, to the second as another's. If Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, it is charged not as another's but as ours; yet each of us, when conceived and born, bears his own person, not Adam's, and is not Adam's surety.
pass_a.268: So I ask you to weigh with me how that first actual sin can be imputed to us truly or falsely, justly or unjustly. It was one singular deed, and it could make a man guilty only as one who commanded it, carried it out, or consented to it. We did not command it or urge Adam to it; we who did not yet exist did not commit it; and we did not actually consent to it before we existed, or while we were still hidden in the womb. Please tell me, then, how it is truly and justly attributed and charged to each of us individually. If your answer is that the hereditary vice which flowed into us from that act is, as it were, the remnants and seed of that sin and a habitual consent of our will, and that therefore it is justly imputed to us, then you fall in with my view: I freely own and teach mediate imputation that follows hereditary corruption and rests on it.

263: CAPUT V. Examination of Cap. III, in which it is asked what it is for sin to be imputed or not imputed. In the third chapter you again set the state of the controversy, and once that is set you digress again, and take it upon yourself to illustrate what it is to impute and to be imputed, and you weigh first the Hebrew word, then the Greek, citing some places of Scripture to that end—to what purpose, or with what design, I do not know, unless perhaps so that you might swell the bulk of your treatise and cover the scantiness of your arguments. Useful enough, perhaps, your illustration would be for the controversy on justification—since Scripture is wont to describe that now by the imputation of faith and righteousness, now by the non-imputation of sin—but for this question which is between us I do not see what it is worth: for there is no place in all of Scripture in which Adam's sin is said to be imputed to us.
264: Therefore it is not asked between us in what sense Scripture employs the word 'to impute' in this question—for it never employs it—but in what sense in my theses (seeing that you have set out to refute them) I denied that Adam's sin is imputed to us, so that that negation of mine may be known whether true or false, and παραλογισμός avoided. At length you conclude that sin is imputed when it is attributed, considered, and held for sin and punished as sin; on the opposite side, that sin is not imputed when it is not considered as sin, but is covered, pardoned, and remitted. Which certainly is not fitted to our question.
265: For when I affirm that Adam's actual sin is not imputed to us, I do not mean by this that that sin is not considered as sin, but that it is covered, pardoned, and remitted to us. (You see that this explanation of yours of 'not imputing' is alien from my mind and from this question.) It is not asked between us whether Adam's sin is forgiven us: such non-imputation is from mercy; but it is asked between us whether of right, from justice, it is imputed to us or not. You doubtless hold that it is not imputed—that is, that it is remitted to the faithful—and yet the same you contend against me is imputed to all men, and indeed so imputed that in all it is punished in act. I do not ask in this place how that punishment consists with justification or remission and the non-imputation of that sin.
266: But, whatever the case, I contend that that actual sin of Adam is not our sin. Therefore it cannot justly be imputed to us. I grant that to impute is to ascribe, to attribute, to write to one's account: but certain things are to be observed in this place—first of all that distinction of imputation into antecedent and consequent, or immediate and mediate, which, when I was setting the state of the question, I explained in Cap. 2, and do not repeat here: I ask you to remember it. Next this also ought to meet our thought: that what is in dispute between us is not any imputation whatever, but a judicial one, which just punishment follows.
267: Now such an imputation of sin is the act of a judge ascribing sin to someone by his sentence—that is, pronouncing someone guilty of a certain sin, and therefore to be visited with punishment. But sin is ascribed to someone either as to a sinner, or as to one who voluntarily sustains the sinner's person, as a surety: to the former as his own, to the latter as another's. If Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, it is ascribed not as another's, but as ours: for each of us, when he is conceived and born, bears his own person, not Adam's, whose surety he is not.
268: Consider with me, then, I ask, and weigh how that first actual sin can be imputed to us truly or falsely, justly or unjustly. It was a certain singular action, which could not make a man guilty except as one commanding, or executing, or consenting. But we neither commanded it, nor advised Adam to it, nor ourselves—who did not yet exist—committed it, nor consented to it in act, either before we were, or while we lay hidden in the mother's womb. Tell me, then, I beg you, how it is truly and justly attributed and ascribed to each of us? If you answer that that hereditary vice, which flowed into us as produced from that action, is as it were the remnants and seed of that sin, and a habitual—so to speak—consent of our will, and that therefore it is justly imputed to us, you will come down to my opinion, who freely acknowledge and teach mediate imputation, which follows hereditary corruption and is founded in it.
